I guess this is my first time ever purchasing a game, then completed the game at the same day (in less than 7 hours). Woah. An achievement. Aside from various games I've tried as playtester. You can watch my full gameplay here https://youtu.be/ez36lTtdP9c or [url=https://www.twitch.tv/videos/1634196168/]here[/url]. In my gameplay, I acquired three good endings: Beldam Rewritten, A Town Reborn, and A New Purpose. I'm also acquired 17/24 achievements, but as everything is in Chinese, I don't know what each achievements means...

Honestly... I'm not that intrigued to purchase the full game after playing the demo. I don't know. Back then it feels like... It lacks something. However, flock of people watching my demo gameplay https://youtu.be/HphgyqpM3VI through my YouTube channel makes me... intrigued, hence I decided to purchase and play the full version. At the same time, I do have enough fund to purchase the game, and it's not that expensive to purchase.
---
For a detective-FMV-esque game... Considering the price, the contents inside, the full duration a player needed to finish the game, I guess... It's priced correctly. It's not too cheap, not too expensive either.

It's clear that the team who developed this game produced-designed-researched-prepared lots of contents to make the game as compelling as possible. How the game tried to keep you as focus as possible also can be seen as how the narration goes, whether from text chats, how the actors acted, voice notes/recordings, and many more. They even included objectives, so for player who probably got lost in the game, could easily check the objectives to stay on the line. Each characters (whether directly communicating with player or no) also have their own distinctive characteristic, and I like it.

The cons probably... Motion sickness. I don't know. I felt dizzy, nauseous, and motion sickness during the video call session with Ruby. Probably as I saw a vertical video moving all the time, yet everything surrounding it are "still". At the same time, as I scroll using my scroll wheel, sometimes it's also makes me feel dizzy, so I have to slow the scrolling speed. Another one... That I don't know if it's actually intentional or no, is the loading speed to choose one out of two options in the final scene, when you video call-ed with Ruby. You have to be SUPER QUICK in deciding what your choice will be, and when the texts were long, you only have like two or three seconds to read and choose. 🤦🏻‍♂️

Aside from those cons, I guess everything is pretty good already. I can't compared this one to previous two predecessor of the same title, SIMULACRA, and SIMULACRA 2, even though I've purchased both months ago when it went on sale. To close, if you have enough money, buy it, and enjoy your 5~6 hours time immersing yourself as a detective in this game.
---
Also.... Damien... DAMIEN... Duh if I'm close with you, I'm gonna kiss you. 💙😚💙

The only character in this game that makes me feel like... He's truly alive. The way he typed, the way he texted, and incorporated those emojisssssss. 💙 Duh I'm head over heels 💙💙💙

Consider this more of a "meh" review. If you like the first two, you will probably enjoy this game. If you are new to the series however, please play either of the first two. This game is a step up in some ways, but a step down in all the important ways. First, let's talk about the improvements.

Pros/Improvements:
+More choices/impact, but barely
+More video and audio (although the video quality is a bit scuffed, but hey it's an indie game)
+Decent puzzles. A bit on the easy side, but so where the first two games.

Cons/Downgrades:
-This is subjective of course, but man do I dislike the story. Some *minor* spoilers ahead (for all three games): [spoiler]The story is about a ghost. TECHNICALLY, it's a simulacra, but not like the previous games. It's more traditional horror, and less tech based like the previous games. The entire gimmick is the game is on the phone, and revolving it around a ghost just doesn't work here.[/spoiler]
-I don't vibe with the characters. Again, this is subjective but I find both Paul and Ruby to be much less interesting then literally ANY of the other characters from the previous games. I can't really put it into words, they just aren't interesting.
-I personally didn't find the mystery as compelling as the first two. Probably because of the same issue I pointed out in my first con.

TL;DR: If this is interesting to you, play the first two games. If you are a fan of the series, $10 is a pretty cheap price for a still pretty decent game, even if it is worse then the first two.

I have mixed feeling about this game. Overall, the story itself is intriguing and I enjoyed the new mechanics. I have one large gripe, and spoilers ahead for all Simulacra games including Simulacra 3.

[spoiler] The monster in this game is only a Simulacra by name alone. As far as I saw, the monster in this game was 100% just a ghost/demon that ended up being called a Simulacra. Previous games featured a possessed phone with the Sim's origins being from a specific app (Spark, Kimera, Flapee Bird). From the way the Sim in this game behaves, there is no specific apps and it seems to be able to manifest itself wherever it wants to and to whomever it chooses regardless of how much that person interacts with the internet. Sim games also had us investigating a victim who we got to know extremely well by the end of the game. This sort of happened through Paul, but not really. [/spoiler] 

If you really want a game that is 100% faithful to the previous entries in the series, I'm sorry to say that this game is not for you. However, it is a very good mystery/puzzle game. I personally enjoyed it.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is back! This series has grown since it first arrived and S3 feels like the biggest game to date. Only slightly longer than previous games, it's a short, contained little story that furthers the Simulacra mythos and gives us a new demon to fight. Once again, the game presents an interesting idea in which society intertwines with technology, using social media, internet, and smart tech to spread rumors, superstitions, and falsities. The Simulacra mythology has always been interesting in it's ability to create a technology-based supernatural horror story that turns out attachment to technology and our internet habits into our biggest dangers and that continues here. 

The gameplay is much the same as previous chapters. This time, however, instead of finding a phone, you're given one by your "partner", who is tasking you with finding the truth behind the disappearance of the phone's original owner and her friend. This, of course, leads into a much bigger mystery. The game has been designed more around PC play, so it seems, and that means production values are bigger and gameplay design is more extensive. Puzzles feel more involving and seem to have more gameplay elements than previous chapters. It's all still fairly straightforward, with puzzles being easy. Dialogue and some action choices continue to drive the game. I will say that I wish more gameplay could have reflected one particular part of the game that felt like it had the biggest and best diversion from the usual for the series. If there is another chapter, I hope that the developers will continue expanding gameplay elements and creating more involved gameplay.

As anyone who has played previous chapters might expect, there's also a lot of not so great elements that have stuck around. The acting continues to leave much to be desired. Considering the low budget, indie nature of the game it's not surprising, nor does it take much away from the experience, but I did find myself chuckling at times when I am sure I was not meant to. There is a lot of campiness here, and that is also in part because of the dialogue. There are also a few grammatical errors that took me out of the game. Overall, I found there to be a certain level of cheese. I also didn't find myself gravitating towards the story like I did previous chapters. There's certainly something interesting about the story here and the focus on yet another aspect of technology and internet culture had a great insight to it, but previous chapters have been more relatable. We've seen a focus on gaming and phone addiction, false internet presence, social media manipulation, and other real world, relatable stories that could feel like they have something very real to say about the player. Expanding the scope here to cover an entire town and having the story's early parts focus on something more supernatural and urban legend-ish created a bit of a disconnect. That is a minor complaint though. I was also a bit disappointed with the ending here. I expected much more from the Simulacra's presence, but it kind of fizzled out in the end. I was hoping for something as effective as S1 and 2, but this one was not quite as scary or intimidating. 

Overall, I enjoyed this chapter. I have embraced the level of camp and very indie production that comes with the game, so getting past that, I can focus on what I enjoy. Those who have enjoyed previous chapters will enjoy this one as well.

review_text_raw:
After enjoying the first two games, I thought I was in for a treat.

Compared to Simulacra 2, there are less characters and the ones present lack personality and development.

The bland story feels removed from its predecessors and could have easily been its own new entry instead of a third game in the series. Here, it feels like the Simulacra was tacked on at the end for marketing purposes.

The interactive video segment (yes, singular, there is only ONE segment) suffers from technical issues. The audio mixing is very different in volume and the videos cut abruptly between the "interactive" parts and the video parts. At first I thought I didn't understand the puzzle correctly. But no. There is no puzzle. It's so mind-numbingly simple it's disappointing. It makes this whole segment feel like a test, an experiment, NOT a fully fledged feature.

As for the "Follow the trail" feature on the city map? It is used twice in the whole game. Once at the very beginning to serve as a tutorial, then once at the very end.

Simulacra 3 is a husk. It feels boring, uninspired, empty and soulless. An extreme disappointment.

review_text_raw:
I just finished my first play through of the game and got what I can assume is the expected good ending. Given the gallery, there seems to be multiple types of endings.

This was... short. Much shorter than 2.

I have about 15 hours in Simulacra 2 while this took 3 hours to finish.

That being said, this was because the puzzles and sleuthing required in Simulacra 2 was more obscure and multiparted than what is presented in 3. The to do list was more hints and solutions than just minor quests this time around as it was more specific and broken into far more steps for greater clarity. This made the game much faster to go through as you almost always knew what to do next and could get huge help from the people you were speaking with. Perhaps this was feedback from how 2 was too obscure and some people felt like they spent hours looking for something entirely not obvious to them so this was added to help with it.

I can see it helping but it made it feel like I really wasnt needed. All these people had literally the answers themselves and all i had was someones phone. Any one else could have figured it out where as in 2 I felt like only I COULD solve it.

The feed has been streamlined and what you unlock instead is barfed at you in large chunks instead of the steady trickle that you get from social media sleuthing like in 2. This however made everything feel less personal. I didnt care about the missing people at all since they had nothing else going for them identity wise. They were footnotes pushed in to move the story along.

There doesnt seem to be a lot of character in this one. Pacing with the characters seem incredibly jarring as you go from casual work associates to suddenly having to answer deep mental health trauma in scenarios that come from left field and not in a natural way. The social media aspects were very lacking as you couldnt explore much except a small town feed.

Its easy to describe a story as 4 acts. The hook, the crescendo, the reveal, then the resolution.

I didnt feel like there was a lot of build up. The hook is the crescendo itself. Going into game knowing people are missing already was not really that interesting. Before I knew it, I found myself collecting pieces to finish the "ritual" to solve the problem. This also did not feel like I was apart of the story or had much agency. All the pieces were given to me because i asked someone nicely. A relationship that was already built by someone I never meet. I take advantage of all his work, his relationships, and his findings, just to ask other people to do the big bits for me. I never perform any of the rituals, I never do any of the fighting, I am way more of a casual observer than someone who held anyone's fate in my hands.

The ending left me really bored as I truly didnt feel what the relationship was between any of the people. The premise is a bit wonky as its a shut in PI type that just made esoteric relationships with various people around town that suddenly become holders of big puzzle pieces.

I am guessing due to pandemic, the development had to cut back because there doesnt seem to be a giant web of possibilities like 2 did, there are very straight cut and dry of live or die decisions and I kept feeling like I could have messed up everything when the wording between two dialogue options were basically the same and you had only 3 seconds to choose.

Some of the UI and UX were confusing. The minigame felt incredibly easy but that made me question if I was getting baited into something but instead it really was just simply as it was presented. It was more tedious than fun because you had to watch some really weird forced acting as you played the truck guy in phasmophobia on a far smaller scale essentially. 

Not as good as 2. Still recommend because it was enjoyable but definitely a weaker production in comparison.

Pacing with the characters seem incredibly jarring as you go from casual work associates to suddenly having to answer deep mental health trauma in scenarios that come from left field and not in a natural way. The social media aspects were very lacking as you couldnt explore much except a small town feed. Its easy to describe a story as 4 acts. The hook, the crescendo, the reveal, then the resolution. I didnt feel like there was a lot of build up. The hook is the crescendo itself. Going into game knowing people are missing already was not really that interesting. Before I knew it, I found myself collecting pieces to finish the "ritual" to solve the problem. This also did not feel like I was apart of the story or had much agency. All the pieces were given to me because i asked someone nicely. A relationship that was already built by someone I never meet. I take advantage of all his work, his relationships, and his findings, just to ask other people to do the big bits for me. I never perform any of the rituals, I never do any of the fighting, I am way more of a casual observer than someone who held anyone's fate in my hands. The ending left me really bored as I truly didnt feel what the relationship was between any of the people. The premise is a bit wonky as its a shut in PI type that just made esoteric relationships with various people around town that suddenly become holders of big puzzle pieces. I am guessing due to pandemic, the development had to cut back because there doesnt seem to be a giant web of possibilities like 2 did, there are very straight cut and dry of live or die decisions and I kept feeling like I could have messed up everything when the wording between two dialogue options were basically the same and you had only 3 seconds to choose. Some of the UI and UX were confusing. The minigame felt incredibly easy but that made me question if I was getting baited into something but instead it really was just simply as it was presented. It was more tedious than fun because you had to watch some really weird forced acting as you played the truck guy in phasmophobia on a far smaller scale essentially. Not as good as 2. Still recommend because it was enjoyable but definitely a weaker production in comparison.

review_text_raw:
Loved the first two games and was very excited to start the third. The prospect of a new setting---getting away from depraved online influencers and into a rural area---seemed neat. And we might even be working against a new threat, be it a new mutation of the Simulacra or perhaps a different monster altogether. 

In the previous two games, you get engaged right away.
 
Game 1 starts with the phone glitching out, emitting eerie sounds the second you touch it. Then, as though haunted, it forcibly opens one video among a dozen corrupted files, showing a brief yet shocking video that teases the main mystery: what happened to Anna and is this phone haunted? The video is fragmented and ambiguous but the victim’s distress is very clear. Her final words? “Don’t come looking for me.” Its immediately intriguing. 

In the second game you're a junior detective at the local precinct. It starts with a meeting between you and the chief, where he confides to you the existence of a secret division within the police department, one which handles unnatural phenomena. He hands you stolen evidence: a phone, from the recently deceased Maya, who's strange death frightened the PD regulars into closing her case prematurely. In light of their unwillingness to discover the truth, the chief tasks you personally with spelunking through the phone to unearth clues. He needs your help because he's an older fellow who's not technologically inclined, while you're the young whippersnapper who's hip with the youths and does the iphones. 

Right away there's a sense of urgency. The department is looking for the stolen evidence, you’re breaking the rules just by having this conversation with the chief, and this secret division desperately needs to furnish some results or risk being shut down by the higher ups. And it’s all up to you.

Like the first installment, there’s some spooky phone glitches which show us something is terribly wrong but doesn’t show us exactly what, baiting the mystery.

To help you along, the chief sets you up with cutting edge, AI based software to help you log clues, disseminate evidence, remote hack the victim’s laptop and restore corrupted files. It was developed to help law enforcement conduct investigations which, in our modern world, are increasingly linked to social technology and personal communications. So it’s at least believable. And it imparts a cool-factor, being given access to exclusive, law enforcement tech.

In game three, you’re just some indistinguishable f*ck from the neighborhood watch group. You’re met with a normal phone and some flat, uninteresting dialogue from Ruby, who decides that the best gambit to enlist your assistance is to belittle you, calling you out as the office coffee b*tch and saying “you might know me, I’m the one who’s always ordering the double tall macchiato” or whatever. As if to imply that you, you loathsome, lowly creature, are so far beneath her station that you could only recognize her by the coffees she sends you to fetch like the obedient mud worm you are.

Then, after nailing down just how useless you are, she inexplicably puts her entire case in your hands. And by “inexplicably,” I mean there’s no reason whatsoever for her to need you or trust you at all. She just heedlessly unloads her project—a project that could very easily get her fired—onto you, who she has just thoroughly disrespected.

You get another scanning tool but unlike the WARDEN app from Simulacra 2, this one feels… shoehorned. It was made by some b*tchless basement dweller named Paul, who looks and acts like a sock puppet, who’s tied his unusual app to the GPS. For reasons.

Like its predecessors, you still get to see a creepy video but its overly long and boring. And entirely too blatant. You get to see the cheesy shadow monster, what’s called “the Beldam” (a dumber name I could not fathom) without any preamble or creativity or teasing. Not only that but you stumble across it like it’s just another YouTube video in the shuffle queue. No spooky glitch, no nameless entity forcing you to look at it. Just.. “oh hey neat.”

Somehow, despite the obviousness of the monster video, when you send it to Ruby she instantly decides to go for a stroll in the very same haunted hallway, alone. Which was so unbelievably obtuse it completely shattered any immersion I’d forced myself to conjure just to make it this far.

To make matters even less interesting, everyone in town already seems to know about the Beldam. It’s on their social media, it’s in their photo reels, one @$$hole even talks about seeing its shape in his latte foam. Seriously, wtf? So there’s nothing special about you discovering its existence. Instead of engaging your morbid curiosity and imagination, it just makes you feel like you’re reading hokey bullcrap about bigfoot in a lowbrow tabloid. 

The real nail in this games’ coffin is: instead of giving us one victim to focus on, who’s distress we can directly witness and care about, we’re hit with a list of missing randos who’s peril is entirely unknown to us. They’re just “missing” y’know… kind of like the plot. 

The only threat it draws our attention to, is that a comically greedy mayor wants to pave over the local farmers market and build a mall. 
Wow. 
Call in the national guard. 
Nothing gets me quaking in my boots like the threat of a shopping mall. 

And even then, it’s just plain text. No video, no room for interpretation or imagination. They just black-and-white spell it out for you. “MaYOr bAd, mAke fARmErs sAD.”

This game completely lacks any of the inspiration and vision that made the prequels special. Feels like a cheap cash grab.

Uninstalled.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra 3 is a game that is genuinely interesting most of the time. Which is about the biggest compliment I can give it. Now the rest isn't all THAT bad, but it's certainly not on par with Sara is Missing or the original Simulacra. It's a found phone game that could've evolve to be so much more, but instead finds itself stuck with more of the same formulaic problems from previous iterations of the game. Here's some spoiler free bullet points on the game. TLDR at the bottom 

The Story. 
The story is easily the best part of the game. It's fairly interesting, if you've played the previous games, you pick up on a lot of what's going on and the game makes some references to them, but it's definitely not necessary to play the previous games. There's enough of a mystery here that it's kinda neat to unravel. 

Horror 
This is easily the weakest part of the game. I can't express how much I hate this asinine "horror" element. Since the last game, I've called it "Powerpoint horror" because there's moments where the phone glitches and it just sits there. You have to click to advance the glitchiness to increase how scary it is or something. I hate to just openly call out something for being bad design, but imagine you're on a roller coaster. The cart ratchets it's way to the top and you're about to go over the edge. Now you have to use a crank on the side of the roller coaster that lowers you down the drop a few steps at a time. Your stomach never drops, you don't get the adrenaline rush, your arm is getting tired from cranking the cart down though. I really wish this series would knock it off. The first game had loud phone call notifications that would make you jump, but sigh in relief, even a creepy unsettling moment here and there, but this one just tries to use super glitchy video effects. Which brings me to my next complaint. 

VFX
The game is at it's best when you're digging around the phone for answers and the dialogue options to guide people around. However, the absolute worst part is when it relies on fmv green screen vfx to tell a story. Look, I know. The budget doesn't really allow for Marvel movie level vfx, but there's a lot of green screen elements, really cheesy animations, and the acting isn't necessarily the best. I think a lot of the scenes could've been done inexpensively practically, but I'm guessing due to production issues, decisions were made to opt in for vfx instead. The "creepy" shadows and overly aggressive "glitchy" effects aren't really adding a lot to the game. 

The sound design is also particularly horrible in one section of the game. When the game is waiting for your response, the ambient sound levels are maxed out, but when you make a selection, the volume drops back down to normal. Not like a HUGE issue, but it's a glaringly obvious one I feel like should've been very easily caught. 

TLDR; 
The game isn't scary at all. It tries too hard and relies on cheesy vfx, cringey fmv (live action) moments, and puzzles that range from incredibly simple to very vague. Overall the story was just interesting enough for me to finish it, but nothing I'm going to talk about a few days from now.

review_text_raw:
My partner got me this game on day of release for my birthday and it was an incredible gift.

Simulacra 3 explores lore from the previous three titles and weaves it together in new ways, whilst the previous three show a clear escalation of Simulacra in terms of power and malevolence all the elements of the previous games are here in one form or another.

The game is shorter and I dare say has less replayability than the others, I suspect being developed during a pandemic has had the greatest impact on that. I enjoyed exploring as much of the game in one sitting as I could with frustration only at one part where a button didn't work the first time I tried it and reloading the game I didn't think to go back and try it for another twenty or so minutes - but like I said, that was day of release and easily fixable.

I can understand some of the dissatisfaction with the game as a lot of the cult following of the Simulacra series is having know real depth of knowledge on what a Simulacra is, where it came from, what powers it and other such unknowns where snippets have only been revealed to the hardcore investigators in previous releases within this series. This game starts to lift that veil more during the core story line and so far I have not found any Easter Eggs that hint at it being a false narrative or having further hidden clues. It all makes sense as a story and makes sense with the lore of the previous games, including iconic phrases and moments from previous games that put certain happenings from previous games in a new light.

That said the new mechanics are fantastic, the spooks were great and the characters emotive despite their individual isolation. I had a lot of fun figuring out whose social media handles were what person we read about in the news and the lore. If you love the Simulacra series this is a fine addition with the potential for both expansion and further games in the series. I am excited to see what the devs will come up with next and going for the rest of the endings and achievements.

There's not much to say about it. Compared to previous games, the third installment is simply bad; like - really really bad. Once again, the personality of the phone received a severe downgrade, lacking those "small touches" to the UI, additional content and fillers, even more than Simulacra 2, making the device feel bland. 

Characters. What can I say... they're just boring and there's so little of them. Except Paul (who is a filthy excuse of a main protagonist), there's really just Ruby who is often irritating, badly written and feels like yet another unimportant character 'cause she lacks true personality and proper development, just like Paul.

The story... was just weird. I really don't understand why the developers chose such an odd concept for this type of game. Simulacra used to be a series about infested apps, often showing them from a bad angle, revealing their negative impact on human life. This time, we get some ghost which haunts an entire town for no particular reason. Just why. It feels so wrong when compared to the concept of all previous games.

The ending of the game was yet another dissapointment. In my case, it ended... just like that, unexpectedly. Like if it was some kind of a demo or something, an unfinished game. 

There's so much wrong with Simulacra 3. It's badly written, with an odd concept and weird story, lazy design and game mechanics. It just feels like an unfinished game that shouldn't have been released in the first place. Previous games, especially Simulacra 1, are better in all aspects. This installment is some kind of a misunderstanding, a literal joke. If I wasn't a fan of the series, I probably wouldn't even finish this game. It's a pure dissapointment. No matter how hard I try, I can't say anything good about it. I simply don't recommend it.

Even with only 3 hours this game feels like it drags on forever. New characters are introduced way late into the game so you don't give a crap about them, and the ones they do use are just one dimensional exposition dumps with nothing interesting behind them. Unlocking new information on the phone wasn't rewarding, and some of the puzzles were way too tedious, looking for a single spec of information in a sea of nothing. I played this with a group and we were all angry when we figured out a puzzle, they just don't work.

Worst part is, this fails as a horror game as well. The scawy ghost is shown to you constantly so there's no fear of the unknown. The repetition of the symbol isn't scary, it's just goofy. The best part of the game is when the background freaked out and that was the only thing with any interest. It lasts a whole 15 seconds. Every video is just a nothing burger with the person 'seeing something in the distance.' Think paranormal activity 2 levels of boring surveillance. 

It fails at horror, fails at a compelling story, no interesting character, and no fun puzzles. It's just nothing. Just play the other 2 games. They ain't perfect, but better than this by a landslide.

review_text_raw:
After enjoying the first two games I thought I was highly anticipating the release for the 3rd one. Sadly this one falls to deliver  anything close to resembling as a interesting/fun game. Even for  9 dollars, at full price. I feel like I wasted money (not rings of power money though). The phone is completely worthless other than what your supposed to do with it at the time, so it doesn't really feel like discovering a person's phone just kinda getting hand held throughout the game. Seems like they went with less "aps" this time, because you use the same ap (atlas) to get from a map feed to a twitter feed. When I called 911 this time around just nothing happens, instead of some somewhat funny dialogue or something else. 411, or dialing 0 also nothing. Trying to call a few people just has calls getting dropped as well which was always kinda a whatever thing, but it's the little things that keep you kinda engaged in story your telling here.

The two characters in the game are very one dimensional. You even though you have the protagonist's  phone you really don't learn anything of interest about this character outside of his drive to stop the plot of the story.  I didn't feel like I was sneaking a peak into his life with loaded with embarrassing messages from maybe his mom,  cringey selfies he taken, or some random thing he bought or really anything that makes the Protagonist feel like a real character. It felt like all information given was utilized to further the plot which made the game feel much more hollow.  

The only other character that you interact with is also just as bland as the main sadly, despite I think the actress trying very hard to work with very bad writing. (I get the lack of pronouns here, but getting called "ROOK" after I just saved your life like a bunch of times was laughable.) Sadly you don't care about saving any of these people, or this town which really feels like the bulk of work was put into. Basically this town is the main character here... Well it's like trying to save Westeros  without meeting anyone who lived there. No one really gives a crap about it. It's actually such a downgrade from either of the previous two games in this retrospect I'm surprised the same company made this game. 

 Nothing was particularly creepy about this one either, Couple times some creepy things happened while I was searching on the phone but it was very minor. The videos that were supposed to be creepy just looked kinda silly, but I understand it's 9 dollars....and  I'm sure there's quite a bit I missed in my first play though, but honestly I have no desire to go back through and get the other "endings" which endings have typically been very weak for the series anyways... I mean could we actually go somewhere with this? I feel like the developers are just trying to milk what was at first a very engaging dynamic and just throwing it into any pot the can stir here. Can like we be maybe a member of an X-FIles unit and maybe we're getting to the bottom of how all Simulcras originated from? or a literal ton of other directions we can actually take??  Sorry on game 3 just having that your phone/ap can kill people is a played out concept. I feel bad writing this, but this game feels so half-assed and disappointing to me who was a big fan of the series I felt betrayed by what should've been a solid stamp on a decent trilogy here.

That being said I really enjoyed the puzzles and hidden secrets, as I did in the previous games as well. It was a challenge at times to continue but not impossible to figure out on my own. Even with the mistakes here and there in the game I would recommend players who enjoy puzzle/investigation games try this one out.

On it's own, this is a good game. Compared to its' predecessors it's arguably lacking, but I think moreso because of the expectations the first two created for the player. 

This game is absolutely less jarring, intense, and/or scary than the first two. The story is dark and there are some creepy videos but at no point was I reeling back from my monitor like the other games. 

There are new mechanics, such as an interactive map with some interesting functionality and a camera surveillance mini-game, but overall it definitely feels like a Simulacra game. The puzzles are relatively straight forward although I did get stuck once or twice, and to be fair difficulty is highly subjective.

The story is told pretty well, again in my opinion, and although I've seen some people criticizing the actors, I thought they were fine. Not exceptional, not terrible, but they did the job and their performance was still strong enough to retain immersion.

Personally, my biggest complaint was having too much control. I was bouncing between apps, reading websites, clicking on things, chatting with characters, watching videos, digging through social media, reviewing evidence, etc with very little interruption or anticipation that something unexpected would happen. The majority of the intense moments was very predictable, or worse, expected. With the previous titles, I was well aware that a) this was not my phone and b) I was being watched and c) something bad could happen at any moment. An hour into this game and I felt like it was just a new version of an iOS that I was slowly learning at my leisure while casually solving a murder mystery. The point is, this feels a lot more like a detective game than it does a unique horror experience, so interpret that as you will.

Again, though, it doesn't mean it was bad. It just wasn't what I (and apparently a lot of people) expected from a Simulacra title. I don't regret the purchase and I still had a good time; just a different kind of good time.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra 3 is the newest instalment in the titular franchise about an entity that enters our world via modern technology. It has the same "unlock secrets in a phone" gameplay as the previous four instalments (yeh theres a lot) and this one is pretty good fun.

Simulacra 3 takes place in the town of Stonecreek with you working as investigative journalist "Rook" working with other residents of the town to look into the disturbing number of missing person cases in the town. The game revolves around trying to find the secrets locked in a cell phone left to you by "Paul" who was looking into the case before going missing himself. As you solve puzzles more info on the phone unlocks and will set you on the path to one of the games endings as you battle the Simulacra entity. 

Puzzle wise this game adds a lot of new mechanics over the others, you must trace people footsteps on a map app, discover secret locations, and by far the best sequence guide a character to escape the entity while looking through CCTV cameras in a house via a home security app. It's excellent well thought out puzzles that for the most part make a lot of sense and just require you to look around and read the phone clearly. Nothing stumped me too hard and everything flowed well. 

The game feels like it has higher production values than the others too with visuals scares being a lot more impressive and well put together in the video sequences than they were before. Excellent stuff that really added to the horror atmosphere all tied together with a decent story that makes sense and doesn't leave loose ends (at least for the good ending, I have not finished all endings). 

Something the franchise suffered with previously was very bad characters that you kinda wanted to die, Sim 3 solves this by making the characters in this either indifferent to you or on rare occasions actually likeable. I did want to save the cast rather than in the second game where I wanted them all to die for being so obnoxious. Next move- make more characters likeable for the fourth numbered entry.

Overall Simulacra 3 is a good entry in the franchise at around 3-4 hours for one run it's def worth a playthrough. Lots of creepy possessed cell phone fun.

To say I was disappointed by this game is quite the understatement. 

Simulacra and Simulacra 2 are two of my absolute favorite "niche" games. It's rare for me to snap games up at day-one prices, but I was so certain Kaigan Games would deliver the goods yet again that I plunged right in for Simulacra 3. 

This game is straight-up boring. The gameplay is a pitiful shell of what Kaigan Games put forward in the previous titles and in Doctor Who: The Lonely Assassins. There seems to be no reward whatsoever to investigating everything everywhere, like there was in the previous games--no times when any of the ancillary "flavor" stuff becomes actually relevant. 

None of the characters have any depth whatsoever and there is never any feeling that your decisions actually impact the game. I actually managed to "save" one of the characters when I was actively looking for options not to do so--something I never even considered in the previous games, where you felt the humanity of every character strongly enough to have SOME desire to save them when they were in trouble. 

I'm not sure if this game was rushed to market just to try to sell the Trilogy on Halloween weekend or what. Whatever the reason for releasing this shell of a game was, I feel extremely let down as a fan and as someone who has been a disciple for this franchise among my friends. 

I hope Kaigan Games gets a chance to rectify this massive misstep. I would hate for this steaming pile to be the last Simulacra game.

I was excited for this game's release, but after playing the game I am admittedly disappointed and cannot recommend this game to others. I will mention that the way the game flows it does appear that they either lost funding, ran out of time or there were other extenuating circumstances that caused this severe drop in quality. However, I don't think this is enough to outweigh my experience playing the game.

I will say I do like the idea behind the story and the execution of the beginning of the game. However, the "live" video calls are executed in the worst way possible. No only do they not feel live as the film cuts weren't edited in a way to feel like they are happening in real time but there is also 0 consequences for going inactive and not inputting anything in time. The game will auto-select the best responses every time. It just kills any feeling that these sections were important - for if they were why wasn't there a no-response option specifically for these sections as well? Literally makes these sections all the less intense or important as you can just walk away and still get the proper info/endings. It feels like you worked for nothing if you did try to react in real time to these sections. Not only that but the puzzles that had the least impact on the overall story were the hardest, while puzzles for key evidence/advancement toward an ending are either forced or way too simple to solve. It made the game feel unbalanced and more frustrating than fun. The ending sequence feels more like a footnote rather than a true ending to the game as well.

I hope the developers of the game take note of the criticisms given for this release and I hope that the next SIMULACRA game will not repeat these mistakes. This is a terrible way to end the series so I hope they will make up for this the next time around. I loved the first two games and I'll admit there was promise in this one that just fell flat for multiple reasons.

review_text_raw:
Was sadly disappointed with this one - I'm a massive fan of the series, but this just didn't grab me.  

This one felt less polished, and also lacked the same sense of horror / dread / suspense that came across in the earlier titles.  The characters were less compelling and felt less real, the story is very much on rails and you can't do much ahead of when you're meant to.  The puzzles are barely puzzles, and some of the novel new formats they tried with interactive video etc just didn't feel interesting, along with the audio not being well mixed.  

The previous titles felt much more like you'd actually found a real phone and were investigating based on the tools available on it.  A lot of the useful stuff you could do with IRIS previously is gone, and now when you're looking at something relevant a large icon appears which you have to hold down, so there's no chance of glossing over relevant info.  This was more of an interactive story with some minor choice elements rather than a detective puzzle and there's no real sense of horror.  

Even the phone simulation elements felt less compelling, even than Sara Is Missing, the precursor / prototype game.  The effort that went into the fake social media app ecosystem in SIMULACRA 2 made the word feel much more real, and I just didn't get the same with the apps in this.  It feels like less effort was made with linkages and quality of content too - the websites aren't particularly navigable, and the bits that are puzzles are made glaringly obvious by the icon interaction mechanic, as well as just looking like puzzles rather than supposed websites.  

If you loved the rest of the series it's maybe worth a look, but otherwise I'd probably not bother.  I'll likely check back in if they make more, because I genuinely loved SIM, and the first two SIMULACRA games, but doubt I'll be revisiting this one for the alternative endings etc.  

I wonder if the core "simulacra" concept has worn out - I'd love something else like Sara Is Missing, where you're still investigating a paranormal story through a found device, but without necessarily fitting into the lore they've been looking to build in this series.

I would give a mediocre rating here, but, for me, there are more negative aspects than positive ones. If you're new to the series, I recommend skipping the first, playing the second, and forgetting about the third.

I liked Simulacra 2 very much, and that was the game I started with. Not liking the first at all, I was hoping for a more second-like game with the third. But, unfortunatelly, that's not the case.

I don't like that the developers didn't include an intro movie like in the second. Who am I? How do I get the phone? Why am I interested in having it? Of course, it is explained during the next minutes within the phone, but there's a reason that games use intro sequences since they had enough capacity to show one, and may it be only text.

Seeing the first videos on the phone, I had the feeling that the actors weren't really into the game concept, but I could live with that if there weren't the big atmosphere-killer: the ghost.

The second game focussed on the invisible threat. The third game includes CGI-monsters, and they killed every ambiance the moment I saw them. Ironically, after seeing the first CGI-ghost, you have the option to reply within a chat: "It could be fake." And of course, I clicked that answer, because it doesn't only look like fake, but it IS fake. And I got an answer from my in-game-partner that made me believe that the developers take their CGI-ghosts seriously: "No, the video isn't edited".

As with every computer generated horror within a movie, it looks artificial and restricts the atmosphere. I always know I'm watching a movie only.

With that in mind, clicking through the webpages, chats, and media, solving sometimes too easy, sometimes nonsense-riddles, feels unsatisfying, because all you will come to see is more of the CGI-illusion. *Spoiler* The ghost's hands in the office - they took away the thrill instantly! *Spoiler end*

I think, there was a peak with the second game that cannot be repeated so easily.

In the third game of the Simulacra series, developers were bound to make amends for misses they made in a second one. They managed to do it, but new weak points nevertheless appeared.

+
The plot and cohesion deserve praise – Simulacra 3 is an intriguing detective game. The story driven by solid logiс, endings based on the intelligible choices of a player. Also, the antagonist's essence is somehow transformed from previous titles, here it is more classic "bad thing from the deep web" but has an interesting avatar in reality. That is a good development, I would be tired of fighting the same virus a third time in a row.

-
Let's not forget that Simulacra is an interactive movie and, as the second word states, a good movie needs good actors. Are they present here? I beg to differ. Even if you are okay with Kaigan Games' obsession with Asian actorship, the two main actors here are nothing more than boring whatever. This problem remains unsolved, and I wish they put more involvement in choosing lead actors. 

+-
The quality AND quantity are both lowered. For the quantity, a producer decides to make a game more focused and not wash away the player's attention. But for the quality it is nothing less than a lacking of time or money: awful greenscreen, brutal video stitching, stuttering – I have to mention that the production is not so hot.

So, this is a half-good movie. I recommend it because the Dev team made a better game after receiving feedback after the previous one. I'm only adding one guess here. I got a hunch that the feedback from the Publisher also wasn't that great, so Kaigan decided to play it safe here: no ridiculous jumpscares, memes, funny videos in-between, ARGs, and so on. The game is focused on the story and finding the clues, and, maybe, some loyal Simulacra fans would not be pleased by that reason.

review_text_raw:
First of all, let me say that I truly enjoyed this game. I had also liked the first 2 games in the trilogy, so I was looking forward to this one. It didn't disappoint. 

For people who want an idea what's going on in it prior to buying: The game is about a missing person. You have his phone. He was investigating other disappearances in the town and had figured something sinister out about them. You are trying to find where he is, what happened to him, what happened to the other people who vanished, and how to stop it from happening again. It is, primarily, a mystery game with a few horror elements. 

Since you have the phone, most of what you are doing is tied directly to it...emails, messages, maps, cameras, phone calls, etc. You won't be the person actually moving around in the world, even though you'll be interacting with them. You will be supporting them by solving codes, puzzles, cracking into websites/security systems, distracting people/entities, etc. 

Now...This is the 3rd game in a series. If you played the first 2 games, I recommend you play this one as well. If you didn't play either of the first 2, you may be a bit lost on what is exactly going on (as there's a similar backstory going on that ties them together). However, it's not 100% necessary to have played them. It would likely be more fulfilling and satisfying, if you did.

What is good about this game? I really enjoyed most of the puzzles. I liked certain sequences (for lack of a better word, without giving too much away) that occur. I liked the female main character. I enjoyed the story. I liked that it tied in with the first 2 games. It was satisfying in length, with achievements on Steam. 

What wasn't so good about this game? There were a couple of puzzles that were pretty obtuse where the solutions were really difficult to find. These were mainly near the end of the game where a LOT of the phone is unlocked and finding one piece of information might be tricky. With no real hint system (other than the fact a couple of people you interact with might be able to give you one), figuring out a couple of the puzzles definitely wasn't easy to do. As an avid enjoyer of previous entries in the series, I was excited to learn that Simulacra has a third game in its mainline series... but there are reasons why this game has largely flown under the radar. 

Spoilers incoming. 

[spoiler]While an interesting concept, the struggle against the Beldam is significantly less compelling than the simulacra we've seen previously. Characters are unlikable - Ruby is a terrible partner and your options with her feel very linear throughout the experience. The new gameplay elements are a mixed bag: while home security footage segment is cool, the map mechanic was deeply frustrating. None of the missing people you're trying to save are particularly interesting or developed; even Paul (the protagonist). The town in "danger" is literally asking for it for the vast majority of the game. The ending felt abrupt and rushed; the final confrontation with The Beldam lacked the gravitas that previous boss encounters do for the series. To be blunt, I would MUCH rather replay the one with fla-pee bird than replay this game... which says a lot cause I HATED fla-pee bird. [/spoiler]


In many ways, this entry lacks the charm and mystery that makes previous games in this franchise enjoyable.  Overall, I was left disappointed and wanting more from the ending I received - unfortunately, I am not compelled by enough the experience to return to it in search of other endings. I rate it [b]no more[/b] than two stars out of five.

review_text_raw:
This is a very soft recommend. 

I'm a big fan of the first two games and this phone detective genre as a whole and I was very excited for this game when it came out, but had put it on hold for some other games I was playing and finally got through it this morning. 

Bullet points incoming: 

- The game itself is just okay. The story is serviceable but isn't as compelling as 1 or 2, as none of the characters really stood out. They just mostly served as quick conversation pieces and possible plot points / beats on your journey rather than actual characters. It's nothing bad, but the severe lack of personality from most of the characters is just a bit of a letdown. 

- Gameplay was good, but definitely not as great as previous iterations. I personally didn't mind the more linear aspect of it (sure more puzzles would've been a lot better), but I felt for what it was doing it hit the mark so to speak.

- I know some people missed the horror element of it, but in reality a lot of the horror elements from the first 2 were cheap jumpscares which honestly I'm glad are gone bc that's all they are. Cheap ways to scare you and make you go BOO. That being said, the lack of ambient noise / other creepy subtle things from the first 2 games are also toned way down, to where this isn't really a horror game to me, but more of a mystery / adventure game. I feel going into it in that mindset may help more.

- Also, just curious, why would you remove the fast text option from Simulacra 2 for any subsequent playthroughs? That made being able to replay the game (if you so choose to or to achievement hunt) WAY easier and tolerable since you didn't have to wait for the slow pacing of the texts to come in. Removing that seems like such a huge misstep and is likely the only reason I won't 100% this one like I did the others bc in total reality, this is the first simulacra game where I don't really feel like trying to go back and do it.

All in all, is the game bad?
No, but it's nothing amazing either.

Is it a step down from the previous 2?
Yes.

Is it a horror game?
In my opinion, no. Consider this one more of a mystery / thriller experience versus horror. 

Would I recommend it?
If you liked the other 2 games, I think you'll still at least enjoy your time enough to get through it once. If you don't like the previous 2, you probably won't care for it and I'd skip it. If you're in the middle, get it on sale and give a try maybe. If you don't like it, you can always return it before the 2 hour mark.

I personally enjoyed the game very much! 
I was skeptical bc of some reviews, but sometimes you shouldn't let that put you off and play a game yourself.  I've been a fan since Part 1 of the games, and I think the ratings depend a lot on people's personal tastes.

The puzzles and interactions were less present in this part, where I have to agree with some, which I personally think is a bit of a shame. I really liked these new features. 

For me, it was an absolutely great 7 hours of gameplay including the good ending, and I'm satisfied. 
Again, I wish the game didn't end. For me it was fun, and the ending blow me away and was well done.
I really like the type of these games and I hope we'll see more in the future.

review_text_raw:
I really wanted to like this game, I really did. 

I loved the previous Simulacra titles, I loved what they did, how they tackled topics of online life from a very different perspective, I loved the variety of characters and the decisions you got to make about them. And mostly, it was just incredibly fun stalking through someone's phone, through social media, seeing other people react to things in realtime, it wasn't 100% convincing, but it made all of it feel a lot more real. And I loved the feeling of danger when getting in contact and confronting the Entities yourself, it was engaging and scary and amazing storytelling.

All of this is gone here.

Let's start with the concept, the previous titles revolved around some current digital topics, online dating, influencers or predatory games. This game mostly drops the digital. It's a ghost story in a town followed through a Maps-App. There's so many topics that could've fit amazingly - NFT's, VR, AR, even Covid and being forced to be home (which admittedly does come up but in a shallow and meaningless way). But we got a Maps-App and a town-mystery, with themes of power, government, community and the interaction of urban myth and history. This too could potentially have been something interesting, but no. 

The story is maybe the most okay part about this game, the town myth is set up nicely, but quite basic, there are some interesting twists and misdirections, and I loved the part about how all of the events started [spoiler]Amy is just a really cool and interesting character[/spoiler]. But many parts absolutely do not work. Some are really forced like [spoiler]when we have to decieve the poor receptionist and cost her her job because Ruby didn't tell us what she was going to do[/spoiler] and the story also doesn't get nearly enough breathing room to work. Especially because you have to work with different characters and convince them of things, yet you've barely interacted before. It doesn't feel like you're participating in a story but playing a bad puzzle game.

The characters are okay-ish, the one you're interacting most with is Ruby and she's written as though you're meant to form a connection, but I just didn't, I didn't feel that much for her or care that much about her, so the emotional core that's built around her just doesn't work. There are some other characters I liked a lot more like [spoiler]Persephone / Damien and Carin[/spoiler] they're fun interacting with and they have personality, but they're also barely there. And even them are just lame compared to the fun interactions with Murillo or unhinged rants of Aria in Simulacra 2, who just felt like real people, with their own desires, hopes, dreams and delusions.

The horror / scary parts are just completely gone. It's so sad, the previous parts could pull you in so much, through the phone glitching or asking invasive or interesting questions, and create a real sense of dread, but here you don't ever feel in danger, because you never are. How would you feel in danger if the Beldam works by [spoiler]ppl seeing graffiti that wasn't there before, or encountering that eye symbol[/spoiler] which are mostly just tied to the real world. Nothing is i.e. indicating you've forgotten time, like that could've been a great point of tension, like a glitch followed by Ruby calling you and asking where you've been the last days. But nothing interesting or scary happens to you. I'd say the most tense sequence was [spoiler]getting Ruby out of Paul's House[/spoiler] but even there you weren't under time pressure, you didn't have to account for it moving, it wasn't challenging at all. Like [spoiler]electronics drew in the Beldam, her phone could've slowly drawn the Beldam towards her unless you activated something else[/spoiler]. And the Beldam itself isn't scary either. The previous Simulacra were always abstract, unfathomable, which made them scary and interesting, but giving the Beldam a bad CGI form didn't do the "horror" any favors. 

The mechanics in the game and the puzzles were also just lame. Most of it is very bland and unoriginal and the Atlas app (maps) is probably the worst of all. It's such a hacked together mess that doesn't make sense as a piece of software, especially the tracking function, and the hints in that function just make everything a lot worse. Like [spoiler]Thomas favorite place gives you the hint with the coffee order. At first I thought, hey there's this dude rating the Beldam locations, maybe I have to bring that in order? Nope. It says something about chronology, maybe I have to sort the ratings by the date posted? Nope. Oh it says something about a specific order in the description, I saw the post like that (@leftOnRead) might it be the places from which this account posted in order? Nope. What I didn't know was that I wasn't far enough and didn't have the grind, park and bus stop on the map yet.[/spoiler] I wasted so much time because of the hint system trying to solve something I couldn't yet.

The previous titles made you feel smart for figuring stuff out, piecing it together, hacking into things, especially because you had a "real phone", from another person, where you just had to circumvent things, but this game does the horrible mistake of dropping all pretenses. It's not a phone from a person missing, it's a puzzle box by a nerd who doesn't wanna give you straightforward information. There's nothing personal in there. NOTHING. No photos, no chats, everything is locked in his fun juiced up Atlas version. You don't try to outsmart technology to gather hidden intel, you have to get around the tedious roadblocks put in place by the informant - why, exactly? At first it's framed like he only had time to send the phone, but then WHY did he make the effort of hiding everything in these tedious puzzles? Especially when he wanted the information to get out and Ruby able to act. The "social media" (everything you get is the social page on the Atlas app) is sadly also incredibly sparse. There's a few posts you can go through, but where in S2 these mattered and you got to know more about the characters and some characters you would later interact with, here in S3 they barely matter at all. They're not engaging to read through, nor interesting discusssions, they're just lame filler. All of the fun of peeking into someone else's life is gone.

I want to have a small aside about presentation, I guess it was produced under Covid and therefore limited and basically all of it is made with greenscreen and really bad integration. The lighting doesn't match properly, the greenscreen is badly keyed and the acting is okay at best, but these are all things I could've forgiven for an interesting, scary, fun, engaging story. They try to do a lot of 3D stuff where the previous games stuck with 2D effects that worked a lot better, because they don't have the budget to do the 3D right.

Then let's finally come to the ending. Navigating the situation was very confusing. [spoiler]You basically have to talk Ruby down to her senses but I had no idea which answers and which reactions meant what. Sometimes she breaks out in this red demonic voice, but it's unclear if that is supposed to be the entity taking more or getting less control.[/spoiler] I had no idea what was going on and even thought I had failed just to discover I actually got the best ending. All of it is then quickly wrapped up, but it fails to leave anything behind about its themes. Everything is magically fine, or everything is incredibly doomed, it's just as empty as the myth of the Beldam itself. It's really sad to see a series I held in very high regard fall off so steeply.

This one takes itself far too seriously while having the weakest story of the three. The novelty and tightness of part 1 are absent which wouldn't be so bad, but gone also are the goofy charms of the cast and various interactions of part 2. Simulacra 3 is stripped down to be a relatively joyless and linear experience.

Thematically, and there is really no nice way to say this, but this game is like a JHorror movie trying to pass its setting off as being in small town America despite it having the least (as in none) American cast and a very clearly JHorror inspired villain. The story would have been much better served if it were just set in Malaysia and based on some kind of Malaysian folklore. It's hard to take the American small town setting seriously when Old MacDonald's farm has the kind of international phone number you might expect in Hong Kong and literally every single character has a different accent from various parts of the globe. Stick to the bundle that has the first two.

review_text_raw:
I'm giving this a positive review because it's still an enjoyable game, but if you're a massive fan of the previous Simulacra games like I am, you may be pretty disappointed by Simulacra 3. The overall design is fine, and the puzzles are fun, even if this game feels significantly easier than the previous Simulacra games (I mean it's really easy to get the good ending on your first try... you'd practically have to be expressly trying in order to not get it).

The worst part of the game is [spoiler]the fact that it's not really a simulacra at all. It's basically just a regular ghost that they're calling a simulacra for some reason. It's not attached to an app or any sort of technology at all. It deviates from the entire idea of the Simulacra series and feels like it doesn't deserve to be a part of the series[/spoiler].

The characters also have much less personality in this game and feel boring compared to the previous games. You never get to know Paul well like you did with Anna and Maya in Simulacra 1 and 2.

[spoiler]The ending scene where you confront the simulacra is also a huge step back from the previous games. In the others, you interact with it directly, and it feels intense and immersive. In Simulacra 3, you're only interacting with it through someone else, and you feel quite removed from the action. These scenes are always the climax of a Simulacra game, so that's quite disappointing.[/spoiler]

Like all previous Simulacra games, Simulacra 3 has multiple endings, but they're just presented as text blurbs at the end, which feels like really cheap and lackluster storytelling, especially for a studio as brilliant as Kaigan Games. I 100%ed all other Simulacra games, including Pipe Dreams, which is pretty hardcore to 100%, but I just didn't have any motivation to do the same with Simulacra 3. If they allowed you to restart the game at particular checkpoints, I would've, but I don't want to play through the entire game again just for some different ending texts and a few achievements that don't feel worth it.

I think this would've been a perfectly great game if it hadn't been tied to the Simulacra series. If Kaigan Games wants to experiment with other types of stories, that's fine, but they taint the new game and the Simulacra series alike when they try to tie them together. Basically, if you're a Simulacra fan, don't treat this as a Simulacra game.

Overall, the experiance feels like the very first game minus the good with itty bitty of the new. Play at your own risk.

I liked it, it's an ok - good game according to my taste and if you played any other games in the Simulacra Franchise (like Simulacra 1/2 or Simulacra - Pipe Dreams [free]) or from the Kaigan Games Devs from Malaysia (like their Dr. Who lost Phone investigation game) and liked them, you'll probably enjoy this one, too (can play them in any order you want, as the stories are isolated and not dependent on each other save for a few minor easter eggs and references, etc.)

It's far from perfect though, my biggest criticism would probably be the drove of spelling mistakes in the English language version. It appears as if the later development has been rushed or the translators were on crunch time and there wasn't a single proof reading or QA-testing for the English language version at least, which just baffles my mind.

Has some nice achievements at least but the sped up version for further play troughs from the earlier games is missing.
Also has a little replayability, but there are a lot less choices / different paths & options you can take than the seocnd game still had.

if you liked this, maybe check out Kaigan Games other games if you haven't played them yet:
Sarah is missing, Simulacra (1), Simulacra: Pipe Dreams (free to play and good intro to see if you'd like this paid one, too), Simulacra 2 and maybe Doctor Who: The Lonely Assassins, which is a similar Lost phone / investigative mystery game.

Like, good? Nah. Also, any jumpscares? Only one. Previous games of series had more.

However, this game is somehow somewhat unique from the rest of the series. I mean, there is indeed cool stuff that impressed me, like Atlas, Vanguard and KillSwitch. I kinda liked the idea of unlocking locations by collecting files, though some of them were hard to unlock. Vanguard is also cool, I really liked the part where Ruby was stuck in Paul's house. This is a game marred by a clear disconnect between what narrative the audience expects, and what the creators want to tell. The original horror executed its concept well with its meta elements that weren't present in this new experience turned "deep narrative" about the gentrification of a small community. Remembering its roots, I could count the amount of horror moments in Simulacra 3 with a single-fingered hand. Rook-your character-crumpling like paper could certainly be seen as horror, with his flimsy attempts to push consequences on those around him.

The puzzles felt immature and insulting at best, while tedious and hintless at worst. These ranging from reading two posts on their limited feed to tracing paths that were directly communicated; a confusing case with reviews mentioning the need to "pay close attention." Surprises in narrative were few and far between, boiling down to the Simulacra coming in like a disappointing WWE wrestler that you wished wasn't part of the new arc. Pushed by "Big Horror" in an otherwise new space.

The mixed art form in the single truly interactive camera segment was exciting, teasing more diverse gameplay segments. Pity. That was all. Truly, a pity, with the acting of Ruby and Paul being a joy to see, reminding me of passionate youth theatre. It fell quickly back to its trudging phone interface that felt like a nightmare for subsequent playthroughs. Getting all the ending cards felt like a punishment rather than a reward.

Please purge your mind of previous entries if you're going to give this a go, and be ready to spend more time reading meaningless social feeds to fish for info used in two more obtuse puzzles. Keep in mind, this remains the most expensive entry in the series.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra 3, developed by Kaigan Games and published by Neon Doctrine, continues the found-phone horror tradition established by its predecessors, delivering an immersive narrative experience centered around digital mystery and psychological suspense. Set in the eerie town of Stonecreek, the game places players in the role of an intern at a local newspaper tasked with assisting investigative journalist Ruby Myers. The central mystery revolves around the disappearance of Paul Castillo, a software developer whose phone becomes the gateway to unraveling the secrets behind his vanishing. By exploring his digital life through texts, photos, videos, and various apps, players are drawn into a chilling tale that combines supernatural elements with a realistic portrayal of modern technology, creating a sense of intimacy and urgency that few horror games achieve.

The gameplay is built around interacting with Paul's smartphone, where every notification, message, and multimedia file serves as a piece of the puzzle. Players navigate through different apps, decode cryptic information, and use hacking mechanics to access deeper layers of the mystery. The real-time progression of events adds tension and immediacy, encouraging quick decisions that influence the unfolding story. This dynamic storytelling approach allows multiple branching endings based on player choices, enhancing replay value and inviting players to revisit the narrative to uncover all possible outcomes. The interface cleverly mimics a real phone’s UI, making the experience feel personal and immersive, as if players are genuinely investigating a missing person’s digital footprint.

Visually, Simulacra 3 stays true to the series' minimalist yet effective design, presenting a realistic smartphone interface filled with authentic-looking apps and multimedia content. The integration of live-action video calls and interactive elements boosts immersion, while the sound design subtly heightens the suspense throughout the investigation. Despite these strengths, some players have found certain puzzles to be ambiguous or overly obscure, which can stall progression and disrupt the narrative flow. The pacing, while deliberately methodical to build atmosphere, may feel slow to those expecting more traditional horror gameplay or quicker resolutions.

Critical reception for Simulacra 3 has been varied, reflecting its niche appeal. While some reviewers praise its atmospheric storytelling, innovative use of the found-phone format, and the effective blend of horror with investigative mechanics, others point out shortcomings in character depth and the occasional frustration with puzzle design. The player community echoes this division, with many appreciating the eerie mood and unique narrative delivery but expressing disappointment over certain gameplay limitations and the game's pacing. For fans of narrative-driven horror and those intrigued by the concept of piecing together stories through digital clues, Simulacra 3 offers a compelling experience, though it may not resonate with everyone.

In summary, Simulacra 3 represents a strong continuation of the found-phone horror genre, delivering a haunting and interactive story that makes clever use of modern technology as a storytelling device. Its immersive atmosphere and branching narrative paths offer a deep dive into mystery and supernatural horror, appealing especially to players who enjoy investigative and choice-driven games. While some gameplay elements and pacing choices might divide opinion, the game stands as a noteworthy title for those looking to explore a psychologically tense and digitally immersive horror experience.

Rating: 6/10

review_text_raw:
This review includes spoilers: 

I really loved Simulacra 1 and 2 and I replayed them right before the 3. within the last couple of days.
And I've gotta say, I really don't like the main simulacrum in this game. It is way less scary to have a literal monster as the main villain instead of something that possesses humans in my opinion. 

There is also a lack of social commentary, because of that. I've always interpreted the first and second game as social commentaries on smartphone / media addiction. The first one dealt with the negative side of dating apps, the second game dealt with being an influencer and addicted to being famous. This entry does none of that. It's not a social commentary on creepypasta / digital horror, like I thought it would be. 

I also think there are weirdly enough several downgrades in comparison to the 2nd game, which was really weird to me. The UI feels unintuitive, none of your decisions really seemed to influence the people around you, there is no character growth. 

The puzzles feel illogical. Maybe I was too dumb for them, but I don't think the game gives you enough hints to figure out what exactly you are supposed to do at certain points. The hint system was also weirdly useless in this game. 

But I really did like the atlas features (except for the tracing route mode) and the "live" segments.

I'm really sorry to leave this review, I still love this franchise as a whole, but this one just wasn't for me.

review_text_raw:
This game released 3 years ago and I never saw anyone play it or talk about it. After playing it for myself, I can see why.

Honestly, the biggest compliment i can give this game is "It's alright." The game still has an interesting mystery to solve like the other ones do but for some reason they really went off the horror with this one. I feel like what made the first Simulacra so good wasn't just the investigating a phone gameplay, it was the horror aspect of it. The jumpscares were good and it genuinely made you uncomfortable with other little details that really added to the experience, and I would say even Pipe Dreams and 2 got this right, but this one was just not scary at all. There was one jumpscare at most and even then it wasn't a good one. 

If you liked the other Simulacra games for how they made you use your brain to work things out, you might like this game? But if like me, you are looking for decent horror, you should just skip this one because there is absolutely none of it here.

review_text_raw: After waiting so long I finally got around to playing this and I can say, the reviews I saw when this first released lied to me. I thought I would hate it but I actually had some fun and got attached to some of the character. I really liked the characters, their stories, and even the town's story. I fell in love with Stone Creek. I did get what I presume to be the best ending and I wouldn't have it any other way (other than maybe 100%ing in the future). The graphics/effects aren't great at times, the dialogue can be a bit flat or weird, some puzzles are a bit annoying, there are a few typos (however knowing how I type I feel that adds to the immersion), and I did experience one crash from staying tabbed out for too long. I can see why some people don't like the game, but just like Stone Creek the game has flaws and charms and I can appreciate it for what it is. The story to me is quite beautiful, while it doesn't have an as Impactful twist that Simulacra 1 does (nor as good horror or effects) I thought the characters and story were much better than Simulacra 2, although I wish there was more connection to those games than just a passing mention. this also could have been a bug but the epilogue and credits didn't have any music but I feel it also gave me a bit of nice silence to reflect on everything. overall, I think the game is worth a try.

im a big fan of the series since the start, and simulacra 3 is my first time i get to try simulacra by myself (i watched markiplier in 1 and 2..mmm fond memories), and to be honest..im kinda disappointed. the fact that not many people play it or talk about sim 3 already show that the game is a bit underwhelming. even 2 years after the game release, i accidentally stumbled on this game and acknowledged its existence.
its a mid game, an "alright" type of game. it doesnt really give me the thrill and anticipation like the first two games. this is just like a puzzle game. horror? almost none. some lights flickering and glitches here and there and thats all. after i finished the game, i told myself "was that all?". i know im a coward but give me some more jumpscares goddammit.
the acting was fine, i guess. some scenes have the cgi and green screens..kinda too obvious...the older games have some really convincing acting and really good cinematography. nevertheless, the cast did their best and they really put their heart into the act.
overall, i think this is the "worst" game in the Simulacra series, but its not a bad game at all. every aspect is worse than the other simulacra games, underwhelming for a simulacra fan like me. if you like puzzle games or just a simulacra fan, yeah, you could try this game out. but if youre expecting horror, jumpscares, or the best simulacra game ever, this is not it.

this game was originally gifted to me like, what a year ago? Yet I never played it, I saw the mixed reviews and decided that I'll just check it out another day. review_text_raw: The weakest of the Simulacra Trilogy by far (even Pipe Dreams felt more comprehensive as a horror experience). It feels like the budget for this game was severely cut. There are many features missing in this game that were present in the previous, the horror elements are few and far between, and obvious bugs still remaining in the game (as of Sept 2026). The audio mixing clearly has issues with some dialogue being so quiet I have to bump up my volume a considerable amount, only later to have my eardrums blasted by one of Paul's vlog videos. The characters have almost no interesting traits and the writing feels flat. Your responses barely seem to matter for most of the game... what happened to being able to lie convincingly to people over texts? Having your character spill the beans about who they are under the slightest bit of pressure takes all the fun out of choosing unique dialogue. Speaking of the dialogue, it is SLOW with no option for increasing text speed- this made getting all achievements an absolute slog. Overall, I expected more from the final entry in this series. I put off playing this game for a long time because the reviews were very mixed, and this sadly confirmed my expectations of the quality of this game. Maybe pick this up if you still want more Simulacra after playing the first two games, but don't expect the same level of quality.
